title: The Word Made Flesh: New 75-Song Advent Playlist
summary: Brett McCracken curates a low-key collection of songs meant to draw you into doctrinal reflection this Advent.
content: Happy Advent! As I do most years, I curated a new playlist of hand-picked songs to help enrich your experience of this sacred season. This year’s playlist is themed “The Word Made Flesh,” inspired by John 1:1–14. Find the 75-song playlist on Spotify or Apple Music . I picked songs that celebrate the mind-blowing theological reality of incarnation, the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (v. 14). The first part of the Gospel of John has always been among my favorite sections of Scripture, and several songs on this playlist pull directly from these profound biblical words. John’s emphasis on the imagery of light also figures prominently in my song selection. Tonally, this is a more low-key, subdued collection of songs, featuring contemplative and instrumental songs meant to draw you into doctrinal reflection. I included a number of sacred choral works alongside new renditions of old carols and hymns like “Hark! The Herald Angels Sing,” “Come Thou Long Expected Jesus,” and the ancient Prudentius poem, “Of the Father’s Love Begotten.” I tried to set a “cozy fireplace on cold December nights” mood, with plenty of jazz, folk, and low-fi sounds (and not much in the way of Christian pop radio). This can be a stressful and harried season, so I picked songs that cultivate calm. I pray the worshipful vibe of this playlist fosters quiet devotional reflection for you and your family as you journey through Advent toward Christmas. title: Christmas Is Good News for the Headline Weary
summary: There’s no better news than the gospel—the message that God sent his Son to die on a cross for our sins and open a way for us to be reconciled to him.
content: Read Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, “Behold your God!” (Isa. 40:9) Reflect When I first started writing for The Gospel Coalition, my editor told me we were going to report good news. We were going to tell stories of where Christians were helping and the kingdom was advancing. We were going to say, “Behold, church, how God is at work in the world!” Neither of us had a lot of confidence it’d work. We have education and experience in journalism, and we know there’s a reason joy, peace, and cooperation aren’t often featured in articles. Nobody reads those stories. There’s a reason joy, peace, and cooperation aren’t often featured in articles. Nobody reads those stories. That’s not because humans are insensitive monsters. It’s because when we read bad news, our bodies react with fight or flight instincts— studies show our hearts beat faster and our skin begins to perspire. We want to understand or process what’s going on, so we click on the link and read past the headline. When we read good news, on the other hand, we have no physiological response. Heart rates and perspiration levels stay the same. Researchers say it’s the same nonresponse we have when we look at a blank screen. For a long time, I was frustrated with God for creating us this way. Why didn’t he make us able to absorb bad news calmly and react to good news with wild, enthusiastic joy? Wouldn’t that be better? Wouldn’t that make Isaiah’s job easier? And John the Baptist’s? And Jesus’s? Wouldn’t that make the church’s job easier? “Behold your God!” we could say to the world. “Isn’t he amazing? Isn’t it wonderful what he has done for us?” And the secular world would shout back, “Hooray! Praise the Lord!” But that’s not how God did it. And only recently did I begin to spot the beauty in his way. First, it’s right that human bodies react with stress and anxiety to news of sin and brokenness in the world. That’s a sign we were made for another world, one that isn’t steeped in corruption and sadness. It’s a testimony that God himself, the One we image, doesn’t ignore evil. The tension we feel is a tiny shadow of God’s reaction when he sees depravity unfolding across space and time. Second, just because we stay relaxed when reading good reports or stories doesn’t mean we’re unaffected. Studies show that when we hear positive news, we’re not only happier but more likely to take action —to respond with compassion and energy to the world around us. There’s no better news than the gospel—the message that God sent his Son to die on a cross for our sins and open a way for us to be reconciled to him. Our good God offers us not only salvation from our past but purpose for our present and hope for our future. Our good God offers us not only salvation from our past but purpose for our present and hope for our future. This good news changed, and continues to change, the world. Out of grateful joy, Christians have become missionaries, started schools, and adopted children. They’ve moved to broken places, given away their time and money, and forgiven those who sinned against them. They’ve preached the gospel, made countercultural choices, and kept doggedly working long before they saw any fruit. Behold, our God! What marvelous things he has done in us, is doing through us, and has planned for us. Respond Consider your news diet. If good news energizes us, how can you limit your bad news intake or find more good news? How can you keep reminding yourself of the good news of the gospel?
author: Sarah Eekhoff Zylstra

title: ‘Confession’ and ‘Ebenezer’: Moral Clarity in Murky Times
summary: New movies ‘Confession’ and ‘Ebenezer’ unmask the ugliness of secular ‘values.’ They celebrate Christian virtue and the way grace transforms a life.
content: Contemporary Hollywood isn’t necessarily known for moral clarity. More often than not, today’s movies look good but lack coherent convictions; they might be artistically excellent but morally bankrupt . Or the opposite can be true. The movies that do have moral clarity are often aesthetically bland: didactic, unsubtle, cheesy. Every so often, though, movies appear that are compelling to watch, artistically strong, entertaining, and morally commendable. Two new releases like this are Confession and Ebenezer . I went into these movies with low expectations, but both surprised me in good ways. They’re very different films tonally and topically. And while certainly not perfect, they share a refreshingly clear moral vision. Both unmask the ugliness and emptiness of secular “values.” Both celebrate Christian virtue and the way grace transforms a life. As we celebrate Thanksgiving in the United States this week, I’m thankful movies like this are still being made. I commend them to you and your family if you’re looking for edifying stories to watch over the holidays. Confession Shows Christian Courage Under Pressure Confession has a cast full of veteran actors (Rob Lowe, James Franco, Emile Hirsch, Nick Nolte, Jennifer Jason Leigh) but couldn’t find a distributor in Hollywood because the movie’s script is written by Ben Shapiro, a well-known political conservative. In the progressive hegemony of Hollywood, you’ll get canceled or blacklisted for associating with or saying nice things about conservative-made movies. Thus, Confession can only be seen on The Daily Wire , and only six film critics (as of this writing) even bothered to publish reviews of it on Rotten Tomatoes . As some reactions to Fjord revealed earlier this year, viewpoint diversity in Hollywood is limited. “Representation matters!” is the mantra, but arguably the most underrepresented viewpoints in Hollywood—religious and political conservatives—continue to be marginalized. Hollywood feels threatened by conservatives bringing their perspectives to art. Why else would it blacklist movies like Confession ? The irony is that Confession is a movie about leftist regimes suppressing dissenting views as a way to maintain narrative control. So perhaps it’s appropriate that the industry’s reaction is proving the movie’s point. Directed by Czech filmmaker Václav Marhoul, Confession is a strange little movie. It feels at times like a filmed stage play. The chamber drama takes place in confined, claustrophobic, dimly lit spaces and is entirely driven by long, lofty conversations about philosophy, literature, art, and politics. It’s like a Richard Linklater film with Russians who speak with American accents. The film’s pacing is slow. And while the performances are good, it’s not an easy movie to watch. Some viewers won’t be able to sit through Confession’ s 130-minute duration, but it’s rewarding if you do. The film’s central protagonist, Alexei (Rob Lowe), is a former literature professor who converted to Christianity and now—in Stalin’s 1938 Moscow—speaks the dangerous truth that “Christ is above the party.” It’s a truth—as prophetic today as it was then—that lands him in the Lubyanka Prison, where he’s interrogated by former student Vladimir (James Franco). Will Alexei relent and save himself, or will he keep his integrity and pay a significant price? At times, Confession reminded me of Sophie Scholl (2005) or A Hidden Life (2019), movies that capture the high cost Christian dissenters pay when they stand up to oppressive secular regimes. Having found Christ, Alexei sacrifices his livelihood and even his familial attachments for the sake of his Savior. Why? Because he believes in truth and beauty beyond this world. Alexei sacrifices his livelihood and even his familial attachments for the sake of his Savior. Why? Because he believes in truth and beauty beyond this world. title: Why I’m Thankful for Evangelical Publishing
summary: The spread of the gospel and the church’s survival isn’t dependent on the state of publishing. But having quality books on spiritual formation, theology, and church practice makes equipping the saints easier.
content: Around a year into my job as books editor for The Gospel Coalition, I crossed paths with my mailman as he lugged yet another box of books to my front porch. “Do you read much?” he asked. I laughed. I receive a steady stream of books, mainly from evangelical presses, that publishers want me to consider for review or promotion. In many cases, when people ask me for a book recommendation on a specific topic, I have a handful of theologically sound and readable options to choose from. But that’s not the case for many Christians around the world. This summer, I travelled to Brazil to teach a graduate course in Christian ethics. Unfortunately, none of my preferred textbooks—the ones that most closely match my approach to ethics—were available in Portuguese. In English, I have half a dozen good options to choose from. I ended up requiring a translation of John Murray’s Principles of Conduct , which is solid but dated. Though more than 47 million Brazilians identify as evangelical and Portuguese is one of the most commonly spoken languages in the world, there are significant gaps among the available Christian resources. The abundance of books that many American evangelicals enjoy is a result of our Protestant heritage, but we shouldn’t take it for granted. Protestant Publishing Christianity is a religion of the book. Not only were early Christians devoted to the texts of the Old and New Testaments, but they also wrote many apologetic and doctrinal texts. Those early Christians were among the first adopters of the codex (what we think of as the book)—one of the rare times that the church has been a leader in technological innovation. Despite claims to the contrary, Christians were also instrumental in preserving pagan literature. As Thomas Cahill argues , “Without the Mission of the Irish Monks . . . the world that came after them would have been an entirely different one—a world without books.” And, of course, the Protestant Reformation was catalyzed by Gutenberg’s invention of movable type, which turned books and pamphlets into mass media. Had Luther’s Ninety-five Theses not been distributed to the masses by German printers, the emphasis on justification by faith alone and Scripture’s final authority might have been much slower to take root. This year, we’re celebrating the 500th anniversary of William Tyndale’s New Testament translation, an accomplishment that helped create the English language as we know it. Famously, Tyndale’s goal was to help the plowboy in the field know more of God than the religious elites did. That required ready access to Scripture and the ability to read, both of which became emphases among descendants of the Reformation. Protestant missionaries helped make rising literacy a worldwide phenomenon. As political scientist Robert Woodberry argues , “[Conversionary Protestants] advocated mass literacy so that everyone could read the Bible and interpret it competently. Their attempt to convert people through education threatened other elites and spurred these elites to also invest in mass education.” Literacy for the purpose of discipleship was a rising tide that lifted all boats. Protestant missionaries helped make rising literacy a worldwide phenomenon. It’s little wonder that American neo-evangelicals like Billy Graham and Carl F. H. Henry made publishing a priority in the 20th century by founding magazines and book publishers. To some degree, the health of a religious movement depends on the availability of religious resources in print. Worldwide Evangelical Publishing Although I was disappointed by the available options for a core ethics textbook in Portuguese, there are reasons to be encouraged about global publishing. While I was teaching in Brazil, I met with a local Baptist pastor who started a new publishing house, Pro Nobis Editora , in 2018 and has since published more than 120 books. Many have been translated from English, but some were written in Portuguese. Another Brazilian publisher, Editora Fiel

title: The Church Needs to Know Its History
summary: Readers of this first volume of ‘Church History for Everyone’ won’t get a complete understanding of church history, but DeYoung provides a doorway through which ordinary Christians can learn to explore primary sources and more comprehensive surveys on their own.
content: Deep in the archives of my Facebook messages sits a note from a widow named Kathy. She thanked me for using church history in our weekly Bible studies. She loved learning about the early-church martyrs and the pilgrims. As a newly minted senior pastor pursuing a PhD in church history, this was the reassurance I needed. Our message thread ended with Kathy describing her chemo treatments. Like Faithful in John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (a story new to her that strengthened her fight with cancer), Kathy endured her trials and entered the Celestial City. I usually have to defend the benefits of history to other pastors and friends of mine—but rarely with church members. I mostly encounter excitement when I direct Christians to our family history. In Church History for Everyone: The Story of Christianity from the Fall of Jerusalem to the Dawn of the Reformation , Kevin DeYoung, pastor of Christ Covenant Church and associate professor of systematic theology at Reformed Theological Seminary (Charlotte), blends rich doctrine with a pastoral tone. It’s the first of two planned volumes. DeYoung writes, “I intend this book to be a popular history rather than professional history, which means I am writing to be understood by ordinary people who are eager to learn but are not experts” (3). He’s successful in that effort. I wish Kathy could have read this book; it’s a church history for the church. History for the Church How is church history for the church actually for the church ? Well, words on a page are costly. Just like a pastor needs to cut more of his preparation and study out of his sermons than he’d like, a church history book for everyday Christians needs to value the reader’s attention. This means accepting that not every believer has the bandwidth to process all the names and details from church history we might want him or her to. There’s so much to digest, and the practical value of these names, dates, and specialized terms often don’t stick in the minds of casual readers. It’s easy for the stay-at-home mom or busy mechanic to delve into a church history book and quickly lose steam. On the other hand, oversimplifying in an attempt to make a book more accessible can move an argument from truth and falsehood. The story of our past needs the proper names, dates, and details to lead readers to experience the fruit of good historical learning. DeYoung attempts a near-impossible task: to write an introduction to church history that’s true (factually sound), good (encourages the church), and beautiful (enjoyable to read). He checks those boxes. Biographical Emphasis The most compelling histories are told through people, not periods. That explains why, “instead of a chronological encyclopedia version of history,” DeYoung takes “a biographical approach” (6). We get stories about figures like Irenaeus, Perpetua and Felicity, Athanasius, and Jan Hus. We read of Hus, As a pastor, Hus was passionate and sometimes hotheaded. His sermons also displayed a witty sense of humor. . . . Compared to most men of his age, he was not poor, but neither did he amass any fortune or have family estates to retire to. Even later when his enemies charged him with many faults and crimes, they never charged him with the typical list of priestly sins: drunkenness, sexual immorality, laziness, or opulence. (351) This approach has downsides, of course. A lot of important information gets left out. However, DeYoung recognizes that “when the author tells a story, there is a better chance that the reader might keep reading” (8). The most compelling histories are told through people. The biographical approach reinforces the fact that history often isn’t just about information transfer. “The goal in telling church history has been—for most of church history—a deliberate attempt at inspiration,” DeYoung observes. title: Help! My Bible Reading Feels Dead.
summary: Every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person.
content: She has read her Bible every morning for 11 years. She journals. She prays through her passage. She has worked through reading plans , study Bibles, and devotional guides. And yet, sitting across from me in my study, she describes her Scripture reading with one word: dead. “I know I’m supposed to feel something,” she says. “But most days it just feels like going through the motions.” I’ve heard this confession more times than I can count from disciplined, sincere believers who do everything right and feel almost nothing. The standard prescriptions haven’t helped: Read more consistently, slow down and observe carefully, and find the application for your day. They’ve tried it all. The dryness remains. In most cases, the problem is a fundamentally misdirected reading method. Method We Were Handed Many of us were taught (implicitly or explicitly) to approach Scripture as primarily a collection of moral lessons, personal promises, and behavioral directives. We come to a passage asking, What am I supposed to do? What does God promise me here? How does this apply to my situation today? Scripture does instruct, promise, and call us to obey. But when this becomes our only lens, when we treat the Bible as a self-improvement manual with divine authority behind it, we’ve misread what kind of book it is. Moralistic Bible reading produces either pride when you keep up with the commands or despair when you cannot. Neither is an encounter with the living God . Moralistic Bible reading produces either pride when you keep up with the commands or despair when you cannot. Puritan writers such as Walter Marshall warned against what they broadly termed a “legal spirit”: treating God’s Word as a taskmaster instead of hearing in it the voice of a Father who acted in history to save a people for himself. Marshall’s classic Gospel Mystery of Sanctification remains the fullest treatment of this danger, and his diagnosis matches the wider Puritan tradition: The remedy was never more effort. It was a clearer sight of Christ. Road to Emmaus Changes Everything On the afternoon of the first Easter, two disciples walked from Jerusalem to Emmaus with shattered hopes and a Scripture they thought they understood. Then a stranger joined them on the road. “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Jesus didn’t give them a new application strategy. He gave them a new reading of the same Scripture they already possessed. Moses, the Prophets, the Psalms—all of it spoke of him. The entire redemptive history of Israel was moving toward him, finding its meaning in him, and flowing from him. The result wasn’t intellectual satisfaction but a burning heart. “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (v. 32). This “burning” is what theologians call the fruit of redemptive-historical reading. When you read Scripture as God’s unfolding story of redemption , traced through creation, fall, promise, covenant, fulfillment, and consummation, every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person. You’re being introduced, again and again, to him. Read the Whole Story Consider what this lens opens up in familiar passages. Leviticus’s sacrificial system, which modern readers so often experience as tedious, becomes luminous when read as the redemptive-historical preparation for the once-for-all sacrifice of the Lamb of God. Every slaughtered animal announces the same truth: Something must die; sin requires atonement; a substitute must bear what the guilty cannot. You arrive at Calvary, and the whole system resolves into its intended meaning. Every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person. The psalms of lament, those raw and disorienting cries of abandonment, take on new weight when you see that the Son of God himself prayed them from the cross.
author: Kim Dang

title: 5 Reasons Why It’s Hard to Discuss Our AI Fears
summary: Christians aren’t remotely ready for the age of AI. Learn more about it and be ready to draw the line.
content: Between the coverage of Jensen Huang’s departure from (and reinstatement at) Nvidia , the cascading failures in large tech companies , and the obvious cracks in critical infrastructure , many people are feeling acute uncertainty about technology . Recent conversations have led me to an uncomfortable conclusion: Most Christians aren’t remotely ready for the era of AI. Here are five complexities that make talking about AI difficult. 1. AI is not monolithic; it is a series of overlapping epochs. The first epoch of AI is the LLM stage (2022–present). This epoch began with the release of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other models. The second epoch is the agentic AI stage that began this year. The epoch marks the introduction of AI bots such as OpenClaw, Grok Bot, and Muse. The third epoch, which hasn’t arrived yet but will likely begin in 2027 or 2028, is the physical AI stage. The beginning of this epoch will be marked by the arrival of robots (think Tesla’s Optimus robot) that use AI to replicate human actions in the wider world. As I have written elsewhere , these epochs will move and change at speeds faster than we can understand. 2. A wise posture toward AI looks different for four groups of Christians. These four groups (more could be added) are parents, pastors and ministry leaders, educators, and marketplace leaders. Each of these groups needs better education on AI. And after they have been educated, some groups may need to use AI more, and some need to use it less. Parents need to learn from the social media era and better protect their kids. We’ve seen how Gen Z was wrecked by social media apps. We can prevent a similar level of harm to Gen Alpha by making sure they’re not overexposed to AI while they’re young. Pastors and ministry leaders need to learn to develop greater discernment toward AI besides “I love it” or “I hate it.” The “I hate it” group needs to recognize legitimate uses for AI, especially in administrative, systematic, and process situations. The “I love it” group needs to know the serious dangers around cognitive off-loading, intellectual and spiritual malformation when using AI for sermon prep, and legal issues surrounding data. Educators, teachers, and administrators—especially those in Christian education contexts—need to better understand the technology and its neurobiological implications on young people. AI skills aren’t hard to acquire. Learning about harnesses, prompt engineering, MCPs, and markdown files on YouTube can take you from zero to 100 in a matter of hours. These tools don’t need to be incorporated in every grade or every subject. The biggest needs in Christian education should be spiritual formation, the cultivation of virtue, the discipline of reading books and long-form media, and the ability to craft analogy arguments that can be defended orally and in writing. For marketplace leaders, they need to know it’s reasonable to use AI for certain things and then not want it anywhere near other parts of your day. That is, admittedly, a difficult tension to hold. Many of us are in more than one of these four groups. It will take a great amount of wisdom to parse how to walk in wisdom with AI at our company and under the roof of our home. We need to learn how to appreciate the tech and how we can use it in one domain while insisting it not seep into another domain. It’s OK to want AI to make breakthroughs in medicine and to not want it break the intellectual supply chain of your pastor’s sermon prep. 3. We’re undereducated and overconfident about the tool we’re using all the time. The average person’s education levels about AI are uncomfortably low. This means low understanding on how this technology works, what it’s good at, what it struggles with, what we should use it for, what we shouldn’t use it for, and how to best use it. It’s OK to want AI to make breakthroughs in medicine and to not want it break the intellectual supply chain of your pastor’s sermon prep. At the same time, many people

title: Leverage Church History for Ministry
summary: Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss how pastors can use church history to strengthen their preaching, encourage their congregations, understand historic Christian beliefs, and learn from believers who have gone before us.
content: Why should pastors care about church history, and how can they use it in everyday ministry? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss why church history is more than a subject for scholars. They share practical ways pastors can draw from Christian biographies, historical events, and the early church to strengthen their preaching and help their congregations grow in faith. title: How to Preach to Workers
summary: The New Testament offers two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching.
content: I still remember the first time I heard a sermon on God’s design for work. Pastor Colin Smith was in a series working through the Ten Commandments, and he’d come to the fourth command about the Sabbath. I was expecting to hear challenging words about rest. So I was surprised when he spent the first half of his sermon talking about work. Because he’s a good exegetical preacher, Smith reminded us to pay attention to the part of the passage we might overlook: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work . . .” (Ex. 20:9). For 16 minutes, Smith preached about God’s design for work. He explained how God modeled work in creation, crafting and making our world like a builder, engineer, and artist. And since humans were created in the likeness of this God, our labors are a significant part of what it means to represent him in the world. Then he started naming regular kinds of work—such as the school crossing guard who creates a zone of safety and protection for children. He shared example after example, even naming those who are were unemployed and looking for work as engaging in a form of dignified labor. They can please God as they trust him to provide and remain diligent to seek out what’s next. At the time, I was working a summer landscaping job between semesters at seminary. I took the job because it was necessary, not because I found it personally fulfilling or spiritually significant. I’d been subconsciously wanting to be done with mowing lawns and picking weeds so I could get back to the important work of studying Scripture. But God used Smith’s sermon to reorient my ordinary labor. Preaching with workers in mind is vital to shepherding a congregation. It reminds church members that work is a primary context for discipleship and helps them work out the implications of God’s Word where they spend a large portion of their time. The New Testament gives two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching. Work as an Illustration of the Kingdom As the eternal, perfect Son of God, Jesus isn’t only Savior and Lord but also the most brilliant teacher the world has ever heard. Therefore, as preachers, we take his pedagogy seriously even as we learn his precepts and mimic his practices. Jesus often proclaims the good news by igniting people’s imaginations and explaining eternal truths in concrete realities, including the body (Matt. 6:22; 7:3–5; 24:7–8), nature (Matt. 6:28–29; Mark 11:23; Luke 17:6), and food (Matt. 13:33; John 6:35, 53–56). But Jesus’s most consistent metaphor for the truths of the kingdom is work and workers. Klaus Issler’s survey reveals that of the 37 parables in the Synoptic Gospels, 32 reference work or workers, representing 22 different work roles. In 25 of the parables, work is a main part of the storyline. Here are examples: The farmer sows the seed (Matt. 13). The faithful manager gives the servants of the household food at the proper time (Luke 12:42). Even an unjust judge will give a persistent widow justice (18:1–8). The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A king going into battle should take counsel to see if he’s strong enough before he a ttacks (Luke 14:31). When Jesus describes what it meant to follow him and live in his kingdom, why does he use the ordinary language of work and workers? First, God’s self-disclosure is often wrapped in the language of work. title: The Gospel Coalition 2026 Book Awards
summary: The Gospel Coalition selects the best Christian books published in 2026 in our annual TGC Book Awards.
content: Paul’s plea to Timothy to bring him his cloak and his books is a powerful reminder of how important books have been throughout Christian history (2 Tim. 4:13). Though death seemed near, Paul still longed to study. Good books can strengthen the soul. Amid the flood of new works published every year, it can be hard to find the sorts of books you would want with you on death row. The Gospel Coalition’s editorial team works hard to identify the best evangelical books published each year. This announcement is the culmination of months of hard work by a big team of book lovers. We receive nominations from publishers in 11 categories. Then our editors work together to recommend finalists in each category. Finally, a panel of judges reads each one carefully before casting their votes. The books are evaluated for the way they offer gospel-centered argument and application; include faithful and foundational use of Scripture, both Old Testament and New Testament; foster spiritual discernment of contemporary trials and trends; and encourage efforts to unite and renew the church. The result is a list of 22 books we recommend as helpful resources for the church and for individual believers. We hope you enjoy and are edified by them. You can find the books in a curated list at a discount in TGC’s online bookstore . Additionally, at the bottom of this article, you’ll find books that TGC has published this year, which were ineligible for our book awards. Congratulations to the winners of the 2026 TGC Book Awards. Andrew Spencer Books Editor Popular Theology Dane Ortlund, Finally Home: The Christian Hope of Heaven (Crossway) This world is beautiful, but it’s broken. Its sorrows remind us that something is terribly wrong; its joys whisper that something unimaginably better is coming. In Finally Home , Dane Ortlund turns our gaze toward that glorious future. With theological depth and the tenderness of a pastor who knows how to speak to weary souls, he brings the hope of heaven down to earth, speaking directly to the sorrows and struggles of everyday life. Here’s a book for Christians who need reminding that suffering will not have the last word, that Jesus will make all things new, and that the best is gloriously yet to come. You’ll finish these pages longing for home—and loving the Savior who will welcome you there. Award of Distinction Brett McCracken, The Wisdom of Sleep: How Rest Reveals God’s Truth and Revives Weary Souls (Zondervan) What if one of the most spiritual things you could do tonight is close your eyes and go to sleep? In The Wisdom of Sleep , Brett McCracken takes an activity we spend roughly a third of our lives doing and reveals its surprising theological significance. Pushing back against our culture’s relentless obsession with productivity, he draws on Scripture, science, and cultural insight to show that sleep isn’t a necessary evil or a strategy for getting more done. It’s a gift from God; a nightly reminder that we’re creatures, not the Creator; and a signpost pointing toward our eternal rest in Christ. Refreshingly practical and richly biblical, this book will leave you more grateful for the gift of sleep and more amazed by the God who never slumbers. Judges: Joshua Chatman, Juan Sánchez, Matt Smethurst, Laura Spaulding Ministry Tony Payne , Let the Word Dwell Richly: The Vital Power of the One-Another Word (Matthias Media) Evangelicals remain steadfastly committed to the ministry of God’s Word. And in our Reformed tradition, the sermon—public proclamation of the Word—rightfully takes center stage in our worship. Yet in our emphasis on expositional preaching, have we overlooked the Word ministry God gives to every Christian? Have we neglected the one-another word the New Testament writers repeatedly commend? Those are the questions Tony Payne answers with biblical clarity and practical insight in this follow-up to his classic with Colin Marshall, The Trellis and the Vine . title: Evening Worship’s Culture-Shaping Power
summary: Don’t wait for the perfect time. Trust the Lord, open the doors, and watch him bless his people.
content: Recently, a friend asked me how things were going at the church where I serve. As I reflected on his question, I was overwhelmed with gratitude. The Lord has been astonishingly kind to our congregation over the past several years. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. Then my friend asked a second question: “What changed?” Like many young churches, our early years included growing pains. We loved one another, but not always patiently. We were starting to believe the right truths, but we were still learning to put those truths into action. I thought of several possible answers: faithful elders, growing families, or the cumulative effect of years of expository preaching. Yet as I contemplated, I realized most of the growth in our congregation started with one small decision. Five years ago, our church began gathering at the close of each Lord’s Day for evening worship. Evening worship isn’t a magic formula for church growth or maturity. Christ alone builds his church, but he does use means. I’m convinced that gathering a second time each Lord’s Day has become one of the most significant means by which Christ has shaped the culture of our congregation. Tyranny of the ‘Perfect Time’ When we planted the church in 2013, we began with Sunday school and morning worship. I always hoped we’d eventually add an evening service, but it never seemed to be a good time. Ministry was demanding, other Sunday evening activities filled the calendar, and I worried about whether anyone would even show up. We were waiting for a perfect season that never arrived. None of my reasons for waiting was foolish, but five years later, I can say without hesitation that the Lord has done exceeding, abundantly beyond all we asked or imagined through evening worship. Here are four ways restoring evening worship has shaped our church’s culture. 1. Double Portion of the Means of Grace The most obvious blessing of evening worship is wonderfully simple: It gives our congregation another opportunity each Lord’s Day to gather around the ordinary means of grace. We gather to hear God’s Word read and preached, to pray, to sing his praises, and to enjoy the fellowship of his people. Taken individually, none of these things seems particularly impressive. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. When we gather a second time, we aren’t inventing a new program; we’re doubling down on the same apostolic diet that sustained the early church: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers (Acts 2:42). Those means of grace didn’t expire with the book of Acts; they’re still our Lord’s chosen means for growing his church (v. 47). Often, the conversation about whether to add an evening service begins with the inevitable question: “Does God require evening worship?” While I understand the nature of the question, we’d do better to have the perspective that evening worship isn’t another box to check or a legalistic obligation to bear. It’s an invitation to feast on the grace God delights to give. 2. Sweet, Unhurried Fellowship Evening worship has brought an unexpectedly sweet blessing: It has knitted our church family more tightly together. Sunday evenings have become a space where relationships are genuinely cultivated and deepened. When people gather only on Sunday morning, there’s an understandable urgency. Families often hurriedly arrive just before the prelude and leave soon after the postlude. Conversations are necessarily brief—our members have children to collect, lunches to prepare, and the looming reality of the workweek ahead. Evening worship changes the pace of church life. People tend to arrive earlier and linger longer. Families invite one another over for a meal between services. Friendships that might have taken years to develop in a morning lobby blossom over a casual Sunday evening dinner. Elders have spontaneous shepherding conversations that could never have been scheduled. Over time, we’ve seen these ordi

title: In the Darkness, Christmas Shines a Light
summary: The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves.
content: Read For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising. (Isa. 60:2–3) Reflect There’s something about a sunrise. It wakes the world. Unlike the jarring blare of an alarm clock, a sunrise quietly whispers “Wake, O sleeper” with the graceful love of a parent rubbing a sleeping child’s back. When the sun rises, the slumbering stir to life. We’ve just spent seven or eight hours dead to the world. Then the sunrise triggers in us what looks like a resurrection. We rise. Certain flowers—daisies, poppies, and the aptly named morning glories—open their blossoms at the sun’s rising. Little by little, empty streets fill and quiet houses stir. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. It’s not surprising that the sun is an oft-used metaphor for God. For he, too, resurrects the dead. He, too, is the Giver of life and growth. He, too, draws all things to himself—such as the trees, which by nature grow upward, toward the sun, their branches like arms raised in perpetual worship. This is the created order. All things were made to be drawn to and sustained by the sun. We were made to be alive insofar as we live, grow, and flourish by solar energy. So too with God. We’re in darkness and death without him. As he bestows his grace on us, we rise to new life. We’re able to grow. Like the sunflower blossom, which turns to follow the sun wherever it’s positioned in the sky, we’re created to look to the Lord, who “will arise upon [us], and his glory will be seen upon [us]” (Isa. 60:2). In a world of darkness, we ache for the light. We wait for the sunrise. All nations, all kings, all people share this in common. The horizon each of us looks to—the nature of the “new day” we await—may be different: A new job. A remodeled home. A regime change. But only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. His is “the true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9). Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled in him. Only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves. The special revelation of Christ reveals a truer light than even the sun: the light that is our eternal life, the light the darkness will never overcome (v. 5), the light that will one day end night as we know it (Rev. 22:5). Respond How is God’s glory seen in your life? How are you reflecting his beauty? In contrast to those who dwell in darkness, how does your life reflect 1 Thessalonians 5:5: “You are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness”?

title: 9 Christians Remain Captive After Kaduna Church Abduction
summary: Nine Christians remain in captivity after gunmen abducted 12 worshippers during a Sunday church service in Kurmin Wali community, Chikun Local Government Area of Kaduna state, according to church leaders. The Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Kaduna state chapter, disclosed the abduction on Tuesday, Nov. 17, two days after the attack on Nov. 15. CAN…   The post  9 Christians Remain Captive After Kaduna Church Abduction  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Nine Christians remain in captivity after gunmen abducted 12 worshippers during a Sunday church service in Kurmin Wali community, Chikun Local Government Area of Kaduna state, according to church leaders. The Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Kaduna state chapter, disclosed the abduction on Tuesday, Nov. 17, two days after the attack on Nov. 15. CAN State Chairman Rev. Caleb Bawa Ma’aji said armed men invaded the community while residents were attending a church service and took 12 worshippers. Three of the victims later escaped and returned to the community, while nine remain with their captors. Ma’aji also reported that five residents were abducted during another attack on Oct. 5. According to him, all five remain in captivity. The latest abduction brings the number of people reportedly still held by kidnappers from the two attacks to 14. Ma’aji criticized the Kaduna State Government’s response to security concerns in the community, saying commitments made by Governor Uba Sani after the October attack had not been fulfilled. He said the governor had promised to establish a security base, construct roads, build a school and provide medical facilities for residents. The CAN chairman called on the state government to take urgent action to secure the release of the 14 captives. He also urged security agencies to intensify rescue operations and ensure the victims return safely to their families. He said repeated attacks and kidnappings had created fear among residents who previously lived peacefully in the community. Kaduna State Police Command Spokesperson DSP Mansir Hassan could not be reached for comment. He did not respond to telephone calls seeking confirmation of the Nov. 15 attack or information about measures being taken to rescue the abducted worshippers. The two abductions occurred in Kurmin Wali within six weeks, according to CAN’s account. The association has called on the state government and security agencies to address the situation and secure the release of those still being held. To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: Church Demolished in India’s Odisha State After Mob Attack
summary: A church in India’s eastern state of Odisha was demolished under the supervision of government authorities the day after its owner reported that villagers had vandalized the building, raising fresh concerns about the treatment of Christian minorities in the region. The Beersheba Church, located in Patraguda village in Koraput district, was damaged on Nov. 21…   The post  Church Demolished in India’s Odisha State After Mob Attack  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: A church in India’s eastern state of Odisha was demolished under the supervision of government authorities the day after its owner reported that villagers had vandalized the building, raising fresh concerns about the treatment of Christian minorities in the region. The Beersheba Church, located in Patraguda village in Koraput district, was damaged on Nov. 21 by a group of men who entered the property with pickaxes and hammers, pulled down a cross, and damaged part of a wall. Durjan Harijan, the local Christian who built the church, filed a police complaint naming seven alleged attackers. The next day, Nov. 22, police and local revenue officials demolished the remaining structure in public view. Harijan told The Indian Express that the church was built beside his home for his family, which he described as the only Christian household in the predominantly tribal village of about 900 residents. He said the land belonged to his father. The church served as a place of Sunday worship for his family and other Christians from nearby communities. Harijan also said that some villagers had begun attending services in recent months, prompting accusations that he was attempting to convert people to Christianity. He denied the allegations and said villagers verbally abused him and his family before the church was vandalized. Seeking Justice Police registered a First Information Report (FIR), the formal document initiating a criminal investigation in India, against seven individuals based on Harijan’s complaint. The charges reportedly include offenses related to property damage and acts committed with common intention. As of Nov. 25, police said the investigation remained underway and did not confirm any arrests. Pastor Franklin Josobonto said he joined about 40 other pastors in approaching the police station on Nov. 21 to seek action against those responsible for the vandalism. He told UCA News that villagers subsequently asked police not to pursue the complaint. Local officials offered a different account of the church’s demolition. Kotpad Tehsildar Parsuram Bhatra told The Indian Express that authorities visited the village after the vandalism report and held a peace meeting. During the meeting, villagers alleged that the church was built on government land. Officials then issued Harijan a show-cause notice asking why the structure should not be demolished. Bhatra said Harijan removed the building after receiving the notice. Kotpad police also stated that Harijan carried out the demolition. However, Harijan disputed that account, saying he was pressured to arrange the machinery and is seeking legal advice about taking the matter to court. The dispute over the land has not been independently resolved. Bhatra said a revenue official had been asked to submit a report on the property and demolished structure, with further action to follow. Christian leaders criticized the circumstances surrounding the demolition, particularly its timing so soon after the reported attack. Bishop Pallab Lima of the United Believers Council Network of India described the action as an alarming failure by local authorities to protect the Christian community. Ismail Patro, general secretary of the National Christian Front, visited Patraguda and said seven Christian families lived in the village. Three families had already left because of fear, intimidation, and persecution, he told UCA News. Patro said Christian representatives planned to approach the district’s senior administrator to request an official investigation and restoration of the church. Growing Hostility The incident comes amid longstanding concerns about anti-Christian hostility in Odisha. Christians account for approximately 2.77% of the state’s population of 42 million, according to figures cited by UCA News. The state has experienced some of India’s most serious episodes of anti-Christian violence. In 2008, coordinated attacks by extremist Hindu mobs in Kandhamal district killed more than 100 Chris

content: Around 8:30 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 15, the courtyard of the Darfur Christian Council church in Gorom Refugee Camp near Juba, South Sudan, became a scene of sudden violence. As worshippers gathered for prayer, a group led by Baqir Muhammad Saleh launched a brutal attack. Stones were thrown, sticks were used to beat people, and some victims were bitten and strangled. “Pastor Daniel Hassan suffered severe injuries: a large part of his left ear was lost to a bite, and the tendon in his middle finger was damaged,” a local bishop who wished to remain anonymous said. “Pastor Samuel Omer received serious blows to the head that caused internal injuries. His wife was beaten in the abdominal area and sustained internal trauma. Brother Michael Yusuf was struck in the nose, while Brother Elias Ibrahim Mohammed was strangled and beaten on the stomach, resulting in minor injuries. Others, including Ahmed Khalid and Fatima Ahmed Khalid, were also exposed to the violence.” This was not the first time the church courtyard had been attacked. On April 17, 2025, Pastor Hassan was shot, sustaining injuries to his thigh and hand. The repeated nature of these assaults has left the congregation shaken and deeply concerned for their safety. “We continue to pray for peace and forgiveness, asking believers to restrain themselves and offer words of love, because the church is a place of holiness and prayer. As the Psalmist writes, ‘Turn from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it’ (Psalm 34:14). Christ teaches us to forgive and to be a blessing even in the face of hatred.” Hassan stated. The Darfur Christian Council serves believers who have already fled conflict and persecution in Sudan. For many, the refugee camp was meant to be a place of relative safety. Instead, the church has become a target. The latest attack has deepened fear among worshippers, many of whom now wonder whether they can gather freely to pray without risking further violence. “We demand that the authorities in the camp provide as much protection as possible to the worshippers,” another victim said. “We also demand that a proper investigation be carried out and that justice be done according to the law. The Lord is a God of justice; ‘He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples with equity’ (Psalm 98:9). We cry out for that justice to be seen here.” Despite the pain and injury, the leaders of the Darfur Christian Council have chosen the path of restraint and faith. They continue to call their people to respond with the love of Christ rather than retaliation, holding fast to the truth that the church must remain a place of peace and holiness even when surrounded by hostility. “Though the attack has wounded our bodies and our hearts, we refuse to abandon the way of the cross,” Pastor Hassan said. “‘The Lord is close to the broken-hearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit’ (Psalm 34:18). We trust him to heal our wounds, protect his people, and turn this suffering into a testimony of his grace.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: 19-Year-Old Christian Farmer in Nigeria Loses Hand in Attack
summary: A 19-year-old Christian farmer, Jesse Monday, lost one of his hands after suspected Fulani herdsmen attacked three young men working on their farmland in Rewienku Village, Miango District, Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau state, on Monday, Nov. 23. The attack reportedly occurred around 3 p.m. when the three young men were working on their…   The post  19-Year-Old Christian Farmer in Nigeria Loses Hand in Attack  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: A 19-year-old Christian farmer, Jesse Monday, lost one of his hands after suspected Fulani herdsmen attacked three young men working on their farmland in Rewienku Village, Miango District, Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau state, on Monday, Nov. 23. The attack reportedly occurred around 3 p.m. when the three young men were working on their farm. Monday sustained multiple machete wounds, and his hand was completely severed during the assault. He is currently receiving medical treatment at an undisclosed hospital. The other two young men escaped without physical injuries, according to a statement issued by the Rewienku Youth Development Association (RYDA). Rewienku is a predominantly farming community in Miango District, part of the Irigwe-speaking area of Bassa LGA in Plateau state’s central region. Residents depend largely on agriculture for their livelihoods. In a statement signed by its general secretary, Comr. Vokwe Joshua Obadiah, RYDA called on the Plateau State Government, Bassa Local Government Council and security agencies to investigate the attack, identify those responsible and prosecute the perpetrators. The association also demanded increased security deployments in Rewienku and surrounding farmlands to protect residents from further attacks. It appealed to the government and humanitarian organizations to provide medical assistance and rehabilitation support for Monday. RYDA urged community leaders, the Rigwe Development Association and the Irigwe Youth Movement to work with security agencies to address threats to residents. The association also appealed to residents, particularly young people, to remain calm, avoid retaliation, and report credible information to security authorities. A Growing Problem According to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA), Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria. The network of militias is responsible for four times more civilian deaths than the two prominent Islamic terror organizations, Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), combined. The study’s findings challenge the commonly held belief that the two organized terror groups kill the larger number of Christians, highlighting the Fulani network’s expanded efforts to target Christians. title: ICJ Issues Historic Ruling on Genocide of Rohingya Minority in Myanmar
summary: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled last week that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority population, marking the first time the world’s highest court has found a state directly responsible for committing genocide. The historic judgment brings international legal recognition to atrocities that killed thousands of people and forced hundreds of thousands…   The post  ICJ Issues Historic Ruling on Genocide of Rohingya Minority in Myanmar  first appeared on  Inter
content: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled last week that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority population, marking the first time the world’s highest court has found a state directly responsible for committing genocide. The historic judgment brings international legal recognition to atrocities that killed thousands of people and forced hundreds of thousands from their homes, while shining a spotlight on the issue of religious minorities facing state-sponsored persecution. In a 9-6 decision, the court found that Myanmar’s military committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine state. The ruling followed a seven-year legal case brought by The Gambia, which accused Myanmar of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention through its treatment of the predominantly Muslim minority. Students of the conflict consider the genocide to be ongoing. The legal definition of genocide requires proof of specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Last week’s ruling reinforces the importance of recognizing patterns of dehumanization, discrimination, and organized violence before they develop into mass atrocities. Important Precedent The court found that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya, inflicted serious physical and psychological harm through widespread sexual violence and other abuses, and imposed measures intended to prevent births within the community. The judges concluded that these actions were carried out with the intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population. The military campaign, which Myanmar authorities described as a counterterrorism operation, drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighboring Bangladesh. Survivors reported mass killings, rape, the burning of entire villages, and attacks on civilians attempting to flee. The United Nations previously documented evidence of systematic violence and concluded that the mmilitary’sactions demonstrated genocidal intent. Myanmar’s military authorities have consistently denied committing genocide, arguing that their operations were directed against armed militants. The court’s ruling rejects that defense and establishes state responsibility for the atrocities under international law. The judgment is significant not only because of its unprecedented legal finding but also because it recognizes the consequences of years of discrimination against a religious minority. The Rohingya have faced decades of restrictions on citizenship, movement, education, and religious practice. Myanmar’s 1982 citizenship law effectively excluded most Rohingya from citizenship, leaving them vulnerable to systematic discrimination and state violence. Buddhist nationalist movements in Myanmar have frequently portrayed the Rohingya as outsiders and threats to the country’s Buddhist identity. Military leaders and nationalist figures have exploited these attitudes to justify discrimination and violence against Rohingya. The atrocities demonstrate how religious intolerance, when reinforced by state power and ethnic nationalism, can contribute to mass violence. The ruling also carries implications for other religious minorities in Myanmar, where the military has continued targeting communities whose ethnic and religious identities differ from those of the country’s Buddhist majority. Attacks on Christians About 20% to 30% of ethnic Karen are Christians, while other groups, such as the Chin, are more than 90% Christian. This overlap of ethnic and religious identity has created a volatile situation for believers. Since the military coup in February 2021, the military has repeatedly attacked predominantly Christian communities, destroying churches, displacing civilians, and killing religious leaders and worshippers. content: A Christian family of eight in the Sukma district of Chhattisgarh, India, was left homeless after Hindu nationalists ransacked and demolished their home on the morning of Nov. 16. During the eviction, the family’s essential household items — including food, clothing, bedding, kitchen utensils, and vital personal documents — were thrown out of their home. The house, belonging to Manglu Sodi and his wife, Hirmibai, was reportedly ransacked and demolished because of their Christian faith. Amid the destruction, 4,000 rupees (roughly $43), about five grams of gold, and a bicycle were stolen before the house was destroyed. Relief in Safe House Fleeing for their safety, the family traveled roughly 40 miles to reach the district headquarters of Sukma, where they were placed in a Safe House. Representatives of the Progressive Christian Alliance (PCA), a rights advocacy group working for the welfare of Christian minorities, coordinated with local pastor Harendra Madiya in Sukma to provide relief for the persecuted family. PCA State Coordinator Patras Balti visited the family to encourage and pray with them, urging them to remain steadfast in their faith despite the severe hardship. Although formal complaints have been submitted to the local police station, the Superintendent of Police (SP), and the district collector of Sukma, no formal inquiry or legal action has been initiated to date. Without their identification documents or savings, the family faces steep hurdles in rehabilitation and rebuilding their lives. Historic Church Building Razed Down In another development, up north of Sukma district, about 300 miles away, a historic church estimated by locals to be roughly 130 years old was demolished in Rajnandgaon district of Chhattisgarh in the past week. The structure was part of the campus of the Missionary Bands of the World Leprosy Hospital (also known as the Rajnandgaon Leprosy Hospital and Clinics), which stood on about 23 acres of government-leased land originally allotted for treating and rehabilitating leprosy patients. The Clearance Operation The demolition followed a lease-cancellation order issued on Nov. 6 by the Rajnandgaon district collector. The demolition drive razed not only the church, but also the old hospital wards, administrative offices, and residential quarters of the leprosy hospital. The administration said the reclaimed land will be used for public amenities, including a sports ground. However, Christian watchdogs are skeptical about the district collector’s action. Christian community leaders urged a clear distinction between the government’s right to recover land over alleged lease violations and the decision to destroy a heritage religious structure. title: Christmas is a Bittersweet Holiday in Iraq
summary: This may come as a surprise, but Christmas is a national holiday in Iraq — ever since the government formally declared it so in December 2018. “It feels like a token move to appear non-discriminatory,” said “Petros,” an Assyrian Christian living in the U.S. with an Iraqi expat family. He added that this “token” celebration…   The post  Christmas is a Bittersweet Holiday in Iraq  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: This may come as a surprise, but Christmas is a national holiday in Iraq — ever since the government formally declared it so in December 2018. “It feels like a token move to appear non-discriminatory,” said “Petros,” an Assyrian Christian living in the U.S. with an Iraqi expat family. He added that this “token” celebration of Christmas “ignores the native traditions” of the region’s Christians and “instead opts for a European-style Christmas” with Santa Claus and various types of Christmas trees that don’t naturally grow in the area. Iraq, which was already celebrating the birth of Christ when most of Europe was still pagan, has among the world’s oldest Christian communities, with the faith arriving in the first century A.D. Petros feels that the Iraqi government’s acknowledgment of Christmas is more of a public relations strategy to deflect from the recent horrors faced by Iraq’s Christians. “Yonita,” an Assyrian woman who is Chaldean Catholic and lives in the U.S., believes the recent recognition of Christmas is financially motivated. “Iraq is trying to rebuild itself,” she said, adding that it might be “taking notes” from more successful countries in the region that have comparatively more religious freedom. Yonita suspects that celebrating Christmas could be an attempt at showing camaraderie with the West. It could also be a way to make the homeland seem more congenial to the many Iraqi Christians abroad. As she pointed out, the Christian Iraqi diaspora tends to be quite well-off financially. “There was a formal call inviting us back to Iraq [to] invest in the rebuilding of the cradle of civilization,” Yonita said. A Sad Reality Whatever the Iraqi government’s true motivation, one painful aspect is hard to deny: By the time Christmas became a national holiday, most Iraqi Christians had already been driven out of their homeland. Conditions were so difficult during the previous 15 years that the country had lost up to 90% of its Christian community. Iraq’s remaining Christians, most of whom belong either to the Chaldean Catholic Church or the Assyrian Church of the East, now comprise less than half of 1% of the country’s overall population. The Christian population had already seen considerable decline during the 24-year reign of former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein, a man of immense sadism. But, for all his homicidal flaws, Hussein — though Muslim by background — was no Islamic extremist. In fact, his longtime right-hand man, Deputy Prime Minister Tariq Aziz, was a Christian, at least technically. It would likely be an exaggeration to say that Hussein cared about the welfare of Iraqi Christians, but the bone-crushing force of his reputation rendered most Iraqis, regardless of their faith, too intimidated to indulge in sectarian hostilities. Petros said that his fellow Assyrian Christians “either liked Hussein for providing stability and jobs, or hated him for killing their family members.” Many of Iraq’s Christians wanted him to stay in power only because they had an acute sense of the mayhem that would erupt after their secular tyrant was deposed. “It’s like the saying goes,” Petros said. “Better to deal with the devil you know than the devil you don’t.” At this point, though, both “devils” have fully acquainted themselves with Iraq. The Rise of Extremism The ousting of Hussein from power in 2003 brought in an era of rising Islamic extremism, most notably with the Islamic State group (ISIS), formerly known as “al-Qaida in Iraq.” Some Iraqi Christians were even accused of collaborating with the U.S. military. As the atmosphere grew increasingly precarious in post-Hussein Iraq, most Christians fled the country, having decided the other options — violent death, forced conversion, or paying a religious tax — were unpalatable. Those who remained were often hunted. In June 2007, in the northern Iraqi city of Mosul, a priest and his assistants were killed right in front of his church. title: Advocacy Efforts for Pakistani Christian’s Release Grow More Urgent
summary: Shahzad Masih has been praying for justice since 2017. He was just 16 years old when he was arrested on false charges, and has been waiting to be hanged since 2022. Nine years later, the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ), through its Pakistani counterpart, the Organization for Legal Aid (OLA), is continuing…   The post  Advocacy Efforts for Pakistani Christian’s Release Grow More Urgent  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Shahzad Masih has been praying for justice since 2017. He was just 16 years old when he was arrested on false charges, and has been waiting to be hanged since 2022. Nine years later, the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ), through its Pakistani counterpart, the Organization for Legal Aid (OLA), is continuing to advocate for his release, Christian Daily International reported. In 2017, Masih was working as a janitor at a hospital when a Muslim coworker asked him about his belief in Jesus. As he explained his faith, he mentioned a comment made by a family friend that was spoken against the Prophet Muhammad, which offended the coworker and ended the conversation. The coworker belonged to Tehreek-e-Tahfuz-e-Islam, a conservative Islamic group in Pakistan. Members of the group heard about their conversation and confronted the Masih. Though he tried to clarify the situation, he was handed over to the police on July 13, 2017, and was questioned without legal representation before being imprisoned. In November 2022, according to Section 295C of the Pakistan Penal Code, he was sentenced to death for the “use of derogatory remarks, etc. in respect of the Holy Prophet.” Since then, he has been waiting to be hanged for his unjust sentence. The United Nations has called for his immediate release, stating that these decisions deny his right to “freedom of expression.” OLA has supported him and filed an appeal for his freedom four times, but the Lahore High Court has yet to hear his case. “Shahzad Masih was just 16 years old when he was arrested, and nine years later, he remains on death row for allegedly reporting someone else’s words,” said CeCe Heil, senior counsel and international legal director for the ACLJ. “We urge Pakistani authorities to uphold fundamental human rights, overturn this unjust conviction, and bring Shahzad Masih home to his family.” One of Many As more stories of Christians being imprisoned for false blasphemy accusations arise this year — including Amir Peter , who was tried before by a Lahore court in 2024 and died in custody in July — ACLJ is committed more than ever to fighting for the life of this young Christian. “This is the ultimate abominable human rights violation, and we’ll take this case all the way to Pakistan’s Supreme Court,” the advocacy group wrote . Open Doors ranks Pakistan as the eighth most dangerous place to be a Christian in the world. They are constantly subjected to persecution through discrimination, death threats, mob violence, imprisonment, and death, through its Pakistani counterpart, the Organization for Legal Aid (OLA), continues. title: Vietnam Demolishes Historic Catholic Property Amid Church Land Dispute
summary: Vietnamese authorities demolished a historic building belonging to the Redemptorist Catholic community in the central city of Huế on Tuesday, escalating a decades-long dispute over church property and raising renewed concerns about religious freedom in the communist-governed country. The demolition of the L’Accueil building followed the deployment of police by local authorities to block roads…   The post  Vietnam Demolishes Historic Catholic Property Amid Church Land Dispute  first appeared on
content: Vietnamese authorities demolished a historic building belonging to the Redemptorist Catholic community in the central city of Huế on Tuesday, escalating a decades-long dispute over church property and raising renewed concerns about religious freedom in the communist-governed country. The demolition of the L’Accueil building followed the deployment of police by local authorities to block roads surrounding the Redemptorist monastery and Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church. Electricity to the area was also cut, preventing some parishioners from reaching the church to attend Mass or express solidarity with the religious community. According to the Redemptorists, heavy machinery began demolishing the structure while priests, religious brothers, and parishioners gathered nearby in prayer. The demolition continued through Nov. 18, leaving the property leveled and fenced off. The Redemptorist Provincial Chapter of Vietnam condemned the operation, arguing that authorities proceeded despite unresolved legal questions and repeated requests to review the property’s ownership. “Justice cannot be established through force, and the truth cannot be erased along with the structures that have been demolished,” the congregation said in a Nov. 17 statement as the demolition was proceeding. Communist Land Takeover The dispute centers on land that the Redemptorists purchased in 1930. According to historical documentation cited by the religious order, Huế municipal authorities formally recognized the congregation’s ownership in 1971. The L’Accueil complex was subsequently developed on the property between 1938 and 1943. It served as a center for educational, cultural, and community activities, housing a library, auditorium, and reading room. A sawmill was also established on the grounds in the 1950s, providing local employment. Following the communist takeover of South Vietnam in 1975, the government’s relationship with religious institutions changed significantly. Church properties throughout the country came under increasing state control, with religious communities frequently losing access to land and buildings they had previously owned. The Redemptorists maintain that they never voluntarily surrendered their rights to the L’Accueil property. They acknowledge that the congregation transferred assets associated with a sawmill to the state in 1978, but argue that the transfer did not include the land itself. Authorities subsequently assigned the property to government-controlled institutions. The remaining parcel, measuring about 2,550 square meters, is currently managed by a local sports vocational school. Recent Efforts The congregation has sought the property’s return since 1994. Its most recent formal complaint, submitted to the Huế People’s Committee on Oct. 24, requested recognition of its land-use rights and clarification of the property’s legal status. Authorities reportedly rejected the complaint in a Nov. 8 response, stating that it had no basis for consideration. A notice posted at the property in October announced plans to develop a public park and parking lot on the site. Local authorities have defended the project as serving public interests, including improving traffic conditions and providing additional green space in a densely populated area. Vietnamese law establishes that land is collectively owned by the people and administered by the state. Government authorities have also invoked a 2003 National Assembly resolution that generally prevents reconsideration of certain land and housing arrangements established before July 1, 1991. The Redemptorists, however, dispute the government’s interpretation of the property’s history and say authorities have not adequately explained the legal grounds for demolishing the building. They have asked officials to publicly disclose the documentation supporting their decision and review the historical records presented by the congregation. title: Trump, Xi, and Putin Meet Amid Deteriorating Religious Freedom Conditions
summary: U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin met Thursday in Shenzhen, China, for an unprecedented trilateral summit, projecting an image of cooperation among three of the world’s most powerful nations but offering few concrete agreements on the conflicts and international issues facing them. The roughly 80-minute meeting produced a…   The post  Trump, Xi, and Putin Meet Amid Deteriorating Religious Freedom Conditions   first appeared on  Intern
content: U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin met Thursday in Shenzhen, China, for an unprecedented trilateral summit, projecting an image of cooperation among three of the world’s most powerful nations but offering few concrete agreements on the conflicts and international issues facing them. The roughly 80-minute meeting produced a joint statement addressing United Nations reform, energy production, international legal authority, and nuclear risks. However, the statement offered no clear breakthroughs on the wars in Ukraine or Iran and made no public reference to religious freedom or the persecution of religious communities in China and Russia. The gathering underscored the importance of direct engagement among world leaders as they seek to manage competing interests, global conflicts, and questions about the future of international order. The summit also offered an opportunity to address concerns affecting millions of people who face persecution for their faith, particularly in countries governed by authoritarian regimes. A Summit Focused on Global Stability The three leaders presented themselves as sharing responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. Their joint statement called for United Nations reform, increased production and supply of petroleum products, and further dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. The leaders also emphasized state sovereignty and the immunity of government officials, declaring that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies should not abuse their authority. The language reflects a shared interest among the three governments in limiting the reach of international institutions, although their respective political, economic, and security priorities remain distinct. Concerningly, this language is similar to that used by China in pushing back on American calls to respect human rights and ensure citizens can freely practice religion. Claiming that these are internal affairs, China rejects what it considers to be overly zealous policing by the U.S. and continues on its path of persecution. Putin described the summit as a new chapter in diplomatic history and praised the opportunity for direct engagement with Trump and Xi. The Russian president also invoked the 1945 Yalta Conference, which helped shape the postwar European order, arguing that international conflicts eventually require countries to recognize realities on the ground. While the leaders expressed interest in dialogue and international stability, their meeting did not produce publicly announced agreements to resolve major conflicts or address underlying tensions between their governments. Religious Freedom Remains a Global Concern For religious freedom advocates, high-level diplomatic meetings represent an important opportunity to raise the plight of prisoners of conscience and religious communities facing government persecution. China, in particular, continues to impose severe restrictions on religious practice. Christians in unregistered churches face surveillance, detention, church closures, and pressure to submit to government oversight. The Chinese Communist Party’s campaign to bring religious institutions under its control has affected Protestant house churches, Catholic communities, Tibetan Buddhists, Uyghur Muslims, and other religious minorities. In recent months, international advocates have urged the Trump administration to raise the cases of imprisoned religious leaders with Xi. Earlier this year, Trump raised the case of Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, founder of Beijing’s Zion Church, during a meeting with Xi. Chinese authorities subsequently released Jin, who later relocated to the United States. However, other Zion Church leaders arrested during the same crackdown remain detained, and no such direct advocacy seems to have occurred at this most recent meeting. The case demonstrated how direct presidential engagement can potentially influence the circumstances
